name: Les Halos de Jupiter Châteauneuf-du-Pape Adrastee 2015
text:
## Les Halos de Jupiter Châteauneuf-du-Pape Adrastée 2015

**The story.** Les Halos de Jupiter is a young project with a cosmic name. It began with the 2007 vintage as a partnership between Philippe Cambie, the noted consultant winemaker, and Michel Gassier, who also owns Château de Nages in the [Costières de Nîmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costi%C3%A8res_de_N%C3%AEmes_AOC). The name refers to the planet [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter) and its halos. Besides two Châteauneufs and a white, the partners make wines from the Côtes du Rhône, [Rasteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Rasteau+AOC&go=Go), [Gigondas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC) and [Vacqueyras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacqueyras_AOC), many of them sold abroad. Philippe Cambie died in December 2021 at 59; Jeff Leve called him "the giant of Châteauneuf du Pape", with a lasting impact on the appellation through his work with many estates ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/les-halos-de-jupiter-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). Among the estates he advised were Le Clos du Caillou and Château de Vaudieu.

**The wine: Adrastée.** Adrastée is 100% old-vine [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), from vines over 100 years old in the famous [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) lieu-dit, the plateau of big rounded stones, the [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s). The grapes are fully destemmed but not crushed, fermented at about 28°C for some five weeks, and then aged for 12 months in one-year-old French oak barrels. Only about 125 cases are made each year, "making it almost impossible to find", as Leve puts it ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/les-halos-de-jupiter-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

The name is astronomical too. [Adrastea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrastea_%28moon%29) is one of Jupiter's small inner moons, discovered in photographs taken by Voyager 2 in 1979. It is named after Adrasteia, the foster mother of Zeus in Greek myth, Zeus being the Greek equivalent of the Roman god Jupiter ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrastea_%28moon%29)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) says Grenache suffered from [coulure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulure) at flowering in 2015 (many flowers failed to set into grapes), so yields were lower but quality very promising, with alcohol higher than in the two previous years. She doesn't expect the 2015s to live as long as the 2016s. [John Livingstone-Learmonth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Livingstone-Learmonth), writing for [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/learn/vintage-guides/rhone-vintage-guides/chateauneuf-du-pape-2015-gigondas-vacqueyras-366743/), called it a generally very good year with robust reds and fine tannins, though some Châteauneuf came out a little "hot", and noted that blends often did better than single-site wines in Châteauneuf this year.

**What the critics say for 2015.**
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/les-halos-de-jupiter-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 95** (from the vintage list on his producer page, checked). He calls Adrastée "a sublime wine produced in a great style".
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 95** (from your CellarTracker list).
- With only about 125 cases made, very few critics have published notes on this vintage. The scores I found quoted for 2015 Halos de Jupiter belonged to the estate's other, blended Châteauneuf, not Adrastée, so I've left them out.

**How it's drinking now.** This is the one to watch. In October 2026 the wine is eleven years old, and your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2020 to 2025, which has already closed. The Wine Cellar Insider says Halos de Jupiter is usually best with 3 to 5 years in bottle and that the best vintages drink well from 4 to 15 years after the harvest, which points to about 2030 at the outside. I'd open this one soon, while it still has its fruit. Decant gently, mainly to leave the sediment behind, and drink it the same evening.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, for freshness and lift; older vintages need only enough decanting to leave the sediment behind ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/les-halos-de-jupiter-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). A large Burgundy-style glass suits a mature Grenache.

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages, barbecue and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus tuna, mushrooms, pasta, eggplant and cheese. For a mature Grenache, my picks are roast lamb with [herbes de Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbes_de_Provence), roast duck with figs, a [porcini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boletus_edulis) risotto, or an aged [Comté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comt%C3%A9_cheese). I'd avoid very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Adrastée, and with 125 cases a year it turns up only rarely with fine-wine merchants and at auction. A bottle in the cellar is a rarity.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V), a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name, "the Pope's new castle". The wine became known as "Vin du Pape" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Phylloxera.** The [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight) louse reached Châteauneuf in the early 1870s, earlier than most French regions, and wiped out the vineyards. Before the First World War, much of the replanted wine was sold to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) as "vin de médecine" to strengthen thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law on 15 May 1936. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both [lavender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavandula) and [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **A consultant's legacy.** Philippe Cambie advised many estates in the southern Rhône. Domaine des Bosquets' Julien Bréchet finished his informal training under Cambie at Château de Vaudieu ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)), and Le Clos du Caillou farmed with his help ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **Halos around Jupiter.** Jupiter really does have rings, faint and made mostly of dust. They include an inner, doughnut-shaped "halo ring", and the moon Adrastea orbits at the edge of the main ring and is thought to be one of its main sources of material ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rings_of_Jupiter); [Adrastea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrastea_%28moon%29)).
- **A moon faster than its planet.** Adrastea is one of the few moons in the Solar System that orbits its planet in less time than the planet takes to turn once ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrastea_%28moon%29)).
- **Cool picking for the white.** For their white Châteauneuf, the partners pick in the cold early-morning hours and start fermenting within 30 minutes of the grapes reaching the cellar, to keep them as fresh as possible ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/les-halos-de-jupiter-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **The famous stones.** Much of Châteauneuf is covered in [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), smooth [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz) stones left by Alpine glaciers and rounded over millennia by the [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne). They soak up the sun by day and give the heat back to the vines at night, and in dry summers they help keep moisture in the soil ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine from [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard), Le Cigare Volant, is named after the tale ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and most wines come in at 14 to 15.5%. Yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare, nearly half what [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine) allows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
